sections.history: Pattadakal, on the banks of the Malaprabha, was where Chalukya kings were crowned, and its monuments were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Sangameshwara is the oldest of them, commissioned by Vijayaditya Satyashraya, who ruled from about 696 to 733 CE. He is said to have installed a Shiva linga named Vijayeshvara after himself, and the temple carries that name beside its present one. Sources differ on the exact years, one placing the start around 720 CE. It was left unfinished at his death, and work went on only intermittently in later centuries. A Kannada inscription tablet of 1162 CE stands at the temple, a reminder of how long it has been in use. It sits between the Galaganatha and Virupaksha temples.
sections.architecture: Sangameshwara is a Dravida temple with a square sanctum, an antechamber and a large pillared hall of about twenty pillars, now partly ruined, with the remains of a Nandi mandapa in front. The Archaeological Survey of India notes that it stands nearer to the Pallava form than its younger neighbours, lacking the projecting sukanasika on the front of the tower. Its tower is an early experiment in a design that the builders of Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna would later refine. Seen beside them, Sangameshwara is the rehearsal, plain and weighty, for the fuller statements that followed.
sections.legends: No single legend is tied to Sangameshwara; its story is a royal one. A king set his own word for victory, vijaya, into the name of the god he installed, Vijayeshvara, lord of victory. The unfinished stones add their own note: even great kings leave work for those who come after. Pattadakal itself carries the memory of coronations, its name pointing to the stone of crowning, and the temple stands as a quiet witness to the dynasty that ruled from here.
sections.festivals: Sangameshwara is a protected monument rather than a temple with a daily round of worship, so it keeps no festival calendar of its own. Maha Shivaratri is the observance most associated with Shiva temples in the region; confirm dates locally. Pattadakal is also known for its annual dance festival staged among the monuments, which is worth checking for when planning a visit.
sections.experience: Walk to Sangameshwara from the Virupaksha enclosure and the difference is immediate: older, plainer, more sober. Stand before the broad, partly ruined hall and look up at the tower, then circle the walls where the stone changes from finished to unfinished. The Malaprabha flows close by, and late afternoon light turns the sandstone gold. It rewards anyone who enjoys seeing a great tradition at the moment it was still finding its form.

visit.timings: Open daily in daytime hours as an Archaeological Survey of India monument and UNESCO site; a single ticket admits visitors to the Pattadakal complex. Confirm current hours and fees locally.
visit.dressCode: No strict dress code applies, but modest dress is appropriate given the sacred character of the site; comfortable footwear helps for walking the open complex.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted across the open-air site; tripods or professional equipment may require permission.
visit.gettingThere: Pattadakal is in Karnataka’s Bagalkot district, about 22 km from Badami, which has the nearest railway station, and around 130 km from Hubballi, the nearest airport. It is usually visited together with Badami and Aihole. Sangameshwara stands inside the Pattadakal monument complex.
